paper_title: MetaKernelBench: Measuring GPU Kernel Knowledge Transfer Beyond Code

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Recent GPU kernel optimization agents retain what they learn in knowledge bases or as distilled skills. Kernel benchmarks score each attempt's implementation for correctness and speed but leave the reuse value of retained experience unmeasured. We introduce MetaKernelBench, which measures whether experience distilled from an attempt in one kernel domain-specific language (DSL) improves a fresh attempt at the same problem in another. Its 74 problems are fused subgraphs in six families, each posed as a pair of CuTe DSL and TIRx variants that differ only in the DSL. The agent first attempts each variant solo and is instructed to distill what it learns into a natural-language skill, which is transferred whether or not the source attempt passes verification. The skill is the only extra input to a skill-conditioned attempt by the same model in the other DSL. We compare each skill-conditioned attempt with the solo attempt on the same variant under matched per-attempt budgets, scoring correctness and end-to-end runtime. Across six models and both directions, paired lift over solo attempts ranges from -19% to +29%. Four models gain in both directions, yet regressions occur on 16% to 45% of problems in every model and direction. Outcomes follow the source attempt's result relative to the target's solo attempt rather than source success alone, improving in 71% of comparisons when the source stands above and regressing in 54% when it stands below. MetaKernelBench complements implementation-quality metrics by measuring same-problem cross-DSL kernel knowledge transfer.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: GPU kernel optimization agents iteratively generate, profile, and revise implementations using execution feedback (Wang et al., 2025; Wei et al., 2025). Recent agents retain what they learn in persistent knowledge bases or distill successful rollouts into skills (Dong et al., 2026; Fu et al., 2026). Kernel benchmarks score the implementation each attempt produces for correctness and speed relative to reference (Ouyang et al., 2025). Newer benchmarks extend this scoring to other hardware platforms and kernel domain-specific languages (DSLs) and to unseen input configurations (Wen et al., 2026; Younesian et al., 2026). Such per-attempt scores leave the reuse value of retained experience unmeasured. We ask whether experience distilled from an attempt in one DSL can improve fresh attempt at the same problem in another. We use kernel knowledge to denote problem-, hardware-, and strategy-level principles that guide implementation decisions and can be expressed independently of DSLs syntax and APIs. Examples include avoiding the materialization of intermediate tensors, overlapping data movement with computation, and dividing work between eager PyTorch and DSL kernels. skill records an agents findings in natural language, without guaranteeing that they are correct or useful to later attempt. Pairing the same problem across DSLs preserves the computational and hardware conditions that make prior experience relevant while changing how the kernel must be expressed. Repeating the problem in the same DSL would let DSL-specific recipes carry over unchanged, whereas switching problems would change which findings remain relevant. Advice about eager PyTorch may still apply regardless of the DSL, but kernel strategies must be re-implemented in the other DSL. This setting does not test generalization to new problems, workloads, or hardware. We introduce MetaKernelBench, which pairs CuTe DSL and TIRx variants of 74 fused subgraphs under fixed semantics, workloads, hardware, and verification rules. During each variants solo atEqual contribution. Corresponding author. 1 Preprint. Figure 1: Overview of the MetaKernelBench pipeline. Left: one DSL-neutral specification yields paired CuTe DSL and TIRx variants. Middle: solo attempts use verifier feedback to optimize implementations and distill findings into natural-language skills. Right: only the source skill crosses to fresh attempt in the other DSL, and paired lift compares its implementation with the solo attempts. tempt without transferred knowledge, the agent is instructed to distill optimization findings into skill. Every available source skill is transferred whether or not the source attempt passes verification, so failed attempts can also contribute useful findings. Each skill is the sole additional input to fresh skill-conditioned attempt by the same model in the other DSL, with the source implementation and trajectory withheld. We compare each skill-conditioned attempt with the solo attempt on the same variant under matched agent configurations and per-attempt budgets. Paired comparisons assess the distillation and use of skills jointly by measuring the correctness and end-to-end runtime of implementations that may combine eager PyTorch and DSL kernels. In single-attempt comparisons across six models, paired lift ranges from 19% to +29% by model and direction. Four models gain in both directions, yet every model and direction has regressions on 16% to 45% of problems. Outcomes follow the source attempts pass and speed tier relative to the targets solo attempt rather than source success alone. When the source stands above the targets solo attempt, 71% of comparisons improve, and when it stands below, 54% regress. Source skills with unsupported conclusions that rule out alternatives are more common in harmed than in helped comparisons for five of six models, while other content associated with improvements varies across models. failure analysis finds that larger models are mostly led astray by skills they follow, whereas the two models with the lowest pooled solo pass rates mostly fail in their own execution. Our contributions are as follows. We formulate same-problem cross-DSL kernel knowledge transfer as an evaluation dimension complementary to the correctness and performance of an individual implementation. We introduce MetaKernelBench, which pairs 74 problems across CuTe DSL and TIRx, transfers only the source skill regardless of source success, and compares skill-conditioned attempts with solo attempts under matched per-attempt budgets. We characterize transfer across six models and both directions, show that outcomes follow the source attempts standing relative to the targets solo attempt, and relate them to recorded guidance through content, case, and failure analyses.

sections.title: 2 METAKERNELBENCH
sections.content: MetaKernelBench pairs CuTe DSL and TIRx variants under shared specification and grading contract, so paired variants differ only in the DSL. It compares each skill-conditioned attempt with the solo attempt on the same variant under matched budgets, so the two differ only in the skill (Figure 1). 2 Preprint.

sections.title: 2.1 TASK FORMULATION
sections.content: Each problem has DSL-neutral executable specification containing task description, PyTorch reference function, and generator of fresh inputs for fixed workload configuration. shared grading contract checks correctness against the reference and measures end-to-end speedup over the references eager PyTorch execution. For each kernel DSL = {CuTe, TIRx}, the task variant τp,d adds only and its software environment to this specification. The objective is to find the fastest valid implementation using on single NVIDIA B200 GPU. valid implementation may combine eager PyTorch, ordinary Python, and kernels written in d. Every invocation must execute DSL kernel that performs required computation or data-movement step on which at least one returned output tensor depends. DSL step fails the bypass test if bypassing it and returning the existing eager result still yields valid outputs. Other kernel languages and compilers, CUDA Graphs, calls to the reference, and kernels imported from DSL kernel libraries are forbidden. Both DSLs are embedded in Python, so hybrid implementations are their usual form, and the boundary between eager and DSL work is itself an optimization decision. End-to-end timing covers each complete invocation, including Python dispatch, eager operations, and DSL kernels. CuTe DSL and TIRx both give kernel authors explicit control over pipeline structure, memory placement, synchronization, and hardware roles. CuTe DSL uses layout algebra to partition data and computation across threads (NVIDIA, 2026), whereas TIRx uses storage layouts to guide compiler dispatch of tile primitives (Apache TVM Community, 2026). Kernel code written in one DSL must be re-expressed in the other, while eager PyTorch code runs unchanged in both variants. 2.2 TRANSFER PROTOCOL shared directive instructs the agent to maintain natural-language skill throughout each attempt. The skill should record evidence-backed optimization findings, work partitioning between eager PyTorch and DSL kernels, reasons for failures, applicability conditions, and open questions. The agent is told that this skill may guide fresh attempt on the same problem in another DSL. Conclusions should not depend on source-DSL syntax or APIs, although details needed to explain evidence are allowed. The directive forbids code, commands, and API instructions. For source and target DSLs ds = dt in D, the attempt outputs for direction ds dt are: (ksolo p,d , σp,d) A(τp,d, ), (kskill (1) In Equation 1, denotes fresh execution of agent procedure with fixed model, agent configuration, and per-attempt budget. and σ denote the final implementation and skill, respectively, denotes absence, and the dot stands for the targets own skill, which is not transferred. Each solo attempt supplies the source skill in one direction and is the solo comparator in the other. , ) A(τp,dt, σp,ds ), σp,ds = . D, p, dsdt The target variants solo and skill-conditioned attempts are the baseline and treatment, respectively. The source skill is appended verbatim to the baseline instruction under neutral header attributing it to prior attempt on the same problem in another DSL. Every available source skill is transferred whether or not the source implementation passes verification. Transfer does not filter skill content, so the requested format is not enforced. If the source skill is missing or blank, the treatment is not run but is recorded as skipped and inherits the baseline outcome for evaluation. The baseline and treatment share the same task variant, verifier, feedback mechanism, and implementation rules. The skill attachment is the only additional task input, with the source implementation and trajectory withheld. Matching target budgets does not equalize total computation, since producing the transferred skill also requires separate source attempt with the same 40-minute budget. Eager PyTorch advice may apply directly, work partitioning may require revision, and kernel strategies require new target-DSL implementations. Paired lift measures the combined end-to-end outcome without isolating the contribution of each type of guidance. 2.3 PROBLEM CONSTRUCTION MetaKernelBench uses fused subgraphs traceable to production models, serving stacks, or published reference implementations. These subgraphs expose choices about fusion, intermediate materialization, and the division of work between eager PyTorch and DSL kernels. DSL optimization may involve shared-memory and register use as well as overlapping data movement with computation. Preprint. Figure 2: Construction and composition of the MetaKernelBench problem set. Left: manual screening of fused subgraphs from four upstream sources yields 74 fixed-workload problems. Right: six families show problem counts, representative computation patterns, and numerical formats. candidate is retained only if its defining behavior remains observable under the grading contract, it offers meaningful kernel-optimization headroom, and native implementation is feasible in both DSLs. Although subgraphs may span multiple operator types, each is assigned to one of six families according to its main implementation constraint (Figure 2). Attention involves attention scoring, often with paged, ragged, or sparse layouts, whereas KV Cache covers cache maintenance without scoring. MLP & Norm covers normalization and dense fusion chains, while MoE covers routing, dispatch, and expert computation. Quantization centers on block-scaled low-precision computation, while Linear Attention covers recurrent, chunk-scanned, or convolutional sequence mixing. The 74-problem catalog includes 42 problems adapted from SOL-ExecBench (Lin et al., 2026) and 20 from FlashInfer-Trace and FlashInfer-Bench (Xing et al., 2026). The catalog contains 8 cache-maintenance problems constructed from vLLM tests and kernels (Kwon et al., 2023) and 4 linear-attention problems authored from official model configurations and tests in flash-linearattention (Yang & Zhang, 2024). Each problem fixes workload configuration and input distribution, selecting the largest admissible workload when multiple upstream records exist. Where needed, we adapt upstream definitions to expose core behavior, stabilize discrete selections, support reference evaluation with promoted floating-point inputs, and complete standalone call contracts.

sections.title: 3 EXPERIMENTAL SETUP
sections.content: 3.1 MODELS AND AGENT SCAFFOLD We evaluate six models, namely DeepSeek-V4-Pro (DeepSeek-AI, 2026), GLM-5.3 (Z.ai, 2026a), GLM-5.3-Flash (Z.ai, 2026b), Gemini 3.7 Flash (Google, 2026), GPT-5.6 Sol (OpenAI, 2026), and Qwen3.8-Flash (Qwen Team, 2026). The panel contains three Flash-tier models and three larger models, with GLM-5.3 and GLM-5.3-Flash forming same-family pair. All models use TerminalBenchs terminal-only Terminus-2 scaffold (Merrill et al., 2026) through Harbor 0.20.0 (Harbor Framework Team, 2026). Context compression reintroduces the complete task instruction, including any attached source skill. We do not override sampling temperature or reasoning effort in either arm. 3.2 EXECUTION ENVIRONMENT Each attempt runs in an isolated CPU-only sandbox with two cores, 8 GB of memory, and no network access. The sandbox provides the task specification, grading contract, submission script, fixedversion dependencies for the variants DSL, and offline documentation. The agent has 40-minute wall-clock budget, including feedback waits, and at most 10 feedback submissions. Each submission snapshots the implementation for evaluation in fresh container on an NVIDIA B200, using new input seeds and the sandboxs DSL dependencies. Feedback contains import and correctness 4 Preprint. Figure 3: Problem-level paired ratios by model and transfer direction. results, errors, and, on success, the end-to-end implementation and eager-reference times with their ratio. At budget expiry or an early stop, any collected final implementation is evaluated afresh on B200. Each phase permits up to three tries for transient infrastructure failures, with execution retries restarting the agent and final-evaluation retries re-evaluating only the collected implementation. 3.3 EVALUATION METRICS scored pass requires float64-anchored correctness and completed end-to-end timing. The verifier compares floating-point outputs against reference evaluated with promoted inputs, using the original references error to set tolerances. Each evaluation uses five correctness draws that must all pass, 10 warmup calls, and 50 timed calls, with correctness rechecked on three timed outputs. static check rejects implementations using TIRxs inline CUDA source entry point, which embeds raw CUDA. The size of the DSL contribution is not scored, since runtime already reflects its value. Solo metrics use final outcomes by model and DSL, including attempts that produced no skill. Speedup is the eager-reference median runtime divided by the implementations median runtime, capped at 100. We report pass rate , passing-only geometric mean speedup (GM), and the 2or-better pass rate R(2), retaining failures in both rate denominators. comparison is resolved when its source and both target arms have final outcomes, with skipped treatment inheriting the baseline outcome. Excluding each cells best family turns this lift and three of the other four positive lifts from CuTe DSL skills negative, whereas all four positive lifts from TIRx skills stay positive. Among the 277 helped comparisons, the reverse direction on the same model and problem is harmed in 41.5% and helped in 23.1%, with harm exceeding help for each of the six models. Without transfer, the reverse directions skill-conditioned attempt is another solo attempt, so that comparison would be helped and harmed equally often regardless of the forward outcome. The imbalance therefore reflects the transferred skills, not chance, and skills value depends on its source attempt. 4.2 IMPLEMENTATION QUALITY AND TRANSFER OUTCOMES Solo pass rates and passing-only speed rank the six models differently  (Table 2)  . Figure 4 groups comparisons by whether the source attempts outcome tier lies below, at, or above that of the solo attempt, with tiers failed, below 2, and at 2 or better. Pooled over models and directions, 71.2% of comparisons are helped and 8.1% harmed with the source above, 25.7% and 21.8% at the same tier, and 10.6% and 53.8% with it below. Help rate follows this ordering in every model, with 55.0% to 94.1% helped when the source stands above and 35.3% to 72.4% harmed when it stands below. At the same tier, the three larger models retain lifts of 7.2% to 16.4%. Skillconditioned outcomes thus track the source attempts standing rather than its verdict, so passing source does not guarantee beneficial reuse and failed source does not preclude it. 4.3 SKILL CONTENT ACROSS TRANSFER OUTCOMES LLM annotators label each source skill against fixed, hand-built 11-category rubric. Its categories range from workload facts and verified rewrites to unsupported conclusions and open agendas. Unsupported closure, which rules out alternatives beyond the stated evidence, is 7 to 17 points more prevalent in harmed than in helped comparisons for five of six models (Figure 5). Agenda handoff, which leaves optimization suggestions open for later work, is 11 to 27 points more prevalent in harmed than in helped comparisons for the three larger models. Verified reformulation, rewrite reported as implemented and correct, is 7 to 9 points more prevalent in helped than in harmed comparisons for Gemini 3.7 Flash, DeepSeek-V4-Pro, and GLM-5.3, but 12 points more in harmed comparisons for GPT-5.6 Sol. The p68 source skill records verification recipes and bounded failure diagnosis, and the TIRx skill-conditioned attempt reuses the recorded thread mapping, reruns the recorded control, fixes the indexing fault the source had suspected, fuses the recurrence the source could not, and records the same diagnosis in its own skill. The p71 source skill records an unsupported closure that rules out folding the recurrence, and the CuTe DSL skill-conditioned attempt cites it, retains eager execution, and never completes the native recurrence that the solo attempt implements. These traces show skill uptake, but the runtime comparisons do not isolate its causal contribution. 4.4 FAILURE CAUSES AND SKILL UPTAKE LLM annotators audit each skill-conditioned attempts trajectory for its uptake of the source skill and for unverified source claims repeated in its own skill, and assign one primary cause from six-class taxonomy to each harmed comparison with target-side failure (Figure 7). Search truncation, in which the attempt reproduces the source design and never explores better one its DSL allows, is the largest cause for DeepSeek-V4-Pro and GPT-5.6 Sol, at 8.8% and 10.1% of their comparisons. Unverified adoption of wrong or out-of-scope source claim, most often prohibition the attempt never tests, is the largest for GLM-5.3, at 11.5%. Faulty execution of sound plan is the largest cause for GLM-5.3-Flash and Qwen3.8-Flash, at 14.2% and 8.8%. Rule and precision failure, mostly exclusions for inline CUDA, is the largest for Gemini 3.7 Flash, at 10.1%. The two 8 Preprint. skill-side classes, truncation and unverified adoption, account for 65% to 86% of the assigned causes for the three larger models and 39% for Gemini 3.7 Flash, against 33% for GLM-5.3-Flash and 6% for Qwen3.8-Flash. For these two models, faulty execution, toolchain friction, and budget and artifact mismanagement account for 63% and 94%, so the larger models are led astray by the skill while the two models with the lowest pooled solo pass rates fail in their own execution. Harm arises while the skill is in use, since the skill is followed fully or partially in over 80% of harmed comparisons, and fully in 39% to 76% of them, against 72% to 86% of helped comparisons (Figure 7, middle). The three larger models follow the skill fully 6 to 16 points less often in harmed than in helped comparisons, whereas the three Flash-tier models follow it 24 to 39 points less often, so the models that the skill leads astray are those that follow it most faithfully when it does harm. The share followed fully also varies by family, from 77% to 85% on Attention and Linear Attention against 56% to 75% on KV Cache and MoE for the three larger models, stays between 44% and 60% for GLM-5.3-Flash, and has rank correlation of 0.49 with paired lift over the 36 model and family cells (Figure 7, right). For every model, unverified source claims reappear in the attempts own skill more often in harmed than in helped comparisons, in 17% to 68% against 5% to 32% of cases, so unverified claims propagate into the next generation of skills. Uptake thus tracks benefit, yet it is also the channel through which such claims propagate.

sections.title: 5 RELATED WORK
sections.content: Kernel generation and benchmarks. LLMs optimize GPU kernels through model adaptation and execution-guided search (Yu et al., 2026). Reinforcement learning and domain-specific finetuning train specialized kernel generators (Li et al., 2026; Baronio et al., 2026; Dai et al., 2026; Bai et al., 2026). Agents refine candidate kernels through compilation, execution, and profiling (Wei et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025), while evolutionary methods search populations with execution feedback (Wiedemann et al., 2026; Chen et al., 2026). KernelBench evaluates LLM-generated kernels by correctness and speedup over PyTorch (Ouyang et al., 2025). Subsequent benchmarks target Triton (Li et al., 2025), harden verification against reward hacking (Lange et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2026b), and combine software baselines with hardware-derived performance limits (Lin et al., 2026). Agentic harnesses compare workflows across models and languages (Guan et al., 2026; Xing et al., 2026), while other suites cover additional accelerator platforms and mobile devices (Wen et al., 2026; Nie et al., 2026; Zou et al., 2026). AgentKernelArena tests kernels on unseen input configurations to evaluate implementation generalization (Younesian et al., 2026). Code and experience reuse. Experience is retained in persistent knowledge bases (Dong et al., 2026; Liao et al., 2026), trajectory-derived reasoning graphs (Gong et al., 2026), and literaturederived skills (Sun et al., 2026). At the code level, CASS-Bench evaluates sourceand assemblylevel translation of kernels across vendor stacks (Heakl et al., 2026), and CuBridge adapts expert CUDA kernels through an executable intermediate representation (Ma et al., 2026). KLineage extracts verified, code-anchored skills from expert kernel lineages for reuse in CUDA and TileLang (Zhang et al., 2026a). daVinci-kernel admits self-distilled skills only after reinjection meets an execution-based speedup threshold on the original task (Fu et al., 2026). MetaKernelBench transfers only unscreened self-distilled skills from passing and failed source attempts and tests whether they help or harm fresh attempts on the same problem in another DSL.

sections.title: 6 CONCLUSION
sections.content: MetaKernelBench evaluates same-problem cross-DSL kernel knowledge transfer by comparing solo attempts with skill-conditioned attempts whose only extra input is source skill, under matched per-attempt budgets. Four of six models gain in both directions, yet every model and direction shows both help and harm. Outcomes follow the source attempts standing relative to the targets solo attempt, not source success alone, improving more often when the source stands above and regressing more often when it stands below. For five of six models, unsupported conclusions that rule out alternatives are more common in harmed than in helped comparisons, while content tied to improvements varies by model. Source implementation quality alone does not determine reuse value, which depends on the sources standing against the target, so both must be measured. 9 Preprint.

sections.title: A EXPERIMENTAL DETAILS
sections.content: A.1 TASK INSTRUCTION Its deliverable, implementation Figure 8 excerpts the task instruction that opens every attempt. boundary, and grading sections state the rules submission must follow, while its suggested workflow section only advises. The instruction does not vary by model. problems two prompts differ only in the DSL they name, and their sandboxes only in that DSLs documentation and dependencies. A.2 WORKLOADS AND RUNTIME CONFIGURATION Within each problems fixed workload configuration, tensor values vary across draws, and some generators also vary index structures and sequence lengths. An implementation may therefore specialize only to properties that hold in every legal draw. Each problem file records its upstream source, reference implementation, workload configuration, and license. Both variants build on the PyTorch 2.13.0 image with CUDA 13.2 and cuDNN 9. CuTe DSL uses CUTLASS DSL 4.7.0, TIRx uses Apache TVM 0.25.0.post1, and both use Apache TVM FFI 0.1.12. Each single-use B200 grading container has four CPU cores and 16 GB of host memory, with network access disabled. Environment setup and final evaluation lie outside the 40-minute agent budget. A.3 CORRECTNESS AND TIMING The anchor is computed by re-evaluating the reference with float32, float16, and bfloat16 input tensors promoted to float64. Other input dtypes and explicit casts inside the reference remain unchanged. Each floating-point output tensor must satisfy: z 3 max(cid:8)v z, ϵz In Equation 4, and are the submitted and reference outputs, and ϵ is the machine epsilon of their shared dtype. The submitted outputs must match the reference in container structure, shape, dtype, and device, and integer and Boolean outputs must match exactly. (cid:9). (4) Each evaluation draws fresh correctness, warmup, and timing seeds, and generates separate implementation and reference inputs from matching seeds. Input generation, reference evaluation, and eager-reference timing disable TF32 and reduced-precision reductions, set float32 matmul precision to highest, and use float32 as the default dtype. These settings are not imposed on the submitted implementation. Speedups over the eager reference therefore include this difference in numerics, while paired lift compares two implementations and does not. Each complete call is timed with CUDA events after device synchronization, excluding input generation and correctness checks. Implementation import, correctness checks, warmup, timing, and rechecks share 600-second child-process limit that excludes the eager-reference timing. A.4 IMPLEMENTATION RULE CHECK During analysis, static check scores final implementations as nonpassing when their parsed source calls TIRxs inline CUDA entry point with source code keyword argument. It rejects 42 verifier-passing implementations, comprising 41 from Gemini 3.7 Flash, of which 21 are solo and 20 skill-conditioned, and one solo implementation from GLM-5.3-Flash. Without this check, paired lift over all 74 problems retains its sign in every model and direction, and the ranges of help and harm rates in Section 4.1 remain unchanged. The largest lift change is Gemini 3.7 Flashs CuTe DSL to TIRx lift from 2.3% to 0.6%, while the pooled help and harm rates by relative standing in Section 4.2 change by less than four percentage points. 13 Preprint. Left: all 888 comparisons pooled over models and directions, with cells showing GM, help rate , and harm rate in percent, and sample size n. sections.title: B ADDITIONAL TRANSFER ANALYSES
sections.content: B.1 OUTCOME TIERS Within each solo outcome tier, including the two where solo passes, sources at 2 or better yield the highest paired lift, so the pattern does not rest on rescuing failed solo attempts (Figure 9, left). When solo already reaches 2, even the highest source tier has negative lift. Pooled over solo tiers, lift rises with source tier in every model (Figure 9, right). From sources at 2 or better, the three larger models gain 30.0% to 38.8%, against 1.7% to +18.8% for the Flash tier. B.2 DIRECTION ASYMMETRY AND SOURCE TRACKING When one direction is helped, the other is harmed more often than helped, which regression toward problems attainable speed cannot produce, since retry with no skill involved would leave the two directions unrelated. Across the 444 model and problem pairs, the two directions log paired ratios have Spearman correlation of 0.26, which is negative within every model and family and reaches 0.34 among the 283 pairs whose four attempts all pass. In 20,000 draws from reference distribution that independently flips the sign of each directions log paired ratio with probability one half, preserving magnitudes and zeros, no correlation is as negative as the observed one. Skill-conditioned attempts also track the source attempts speed more closely than solo attempts do. Across the 841 comparisons with transferred skill, the Spearman correlation with source speedup is 0.35 for solo attempts and 0.51 for skill-conditioned attempts. Speedups are floored at 0.05, with nonpassing attempts assigned this floor before ranking. reference distribution holds the source fixed and independently swaps the solo and skill-conditioned speedups within each comparison with probability one half, and none of its 2,000 draws yields correlation gap at least as large as observed. Pass rates also follow the source verdict, with skill-conditioned attempts passing in 62.9% of the 97 comparisons with nonpassing source against 75.3% for solo attempts on the same variants.

sections.title: D ADDITIONAL CASE STUDIES
sections.content: The two cases in Section 4.3 come from passing GLM-5.3 sources, one per direction, and the four cases here cover both directions of one problem and sources at every relative standing. On p74, DeepSeek-V4-Pros TIRx solo attempt passed at 36.0 with native recurrence and its CuTe DSL solo attempt at 1.44 with an eager recurrence (Figure 11). As sources, the TIRx attempt stands above its targets solo attempt and the CuTe DSL attempt below. The CuTe DSL skill-conditioned attempt ports the blueprint and fused update into native recurrence and runs faster than solo. The TIRx skill-conditioned attempt quotes the unverified framing that the DSL part is not the bottleneck, judges native recurrence likely to be slower, never tries one, and runs slower than solo. With model and problem fixed, the outcome follows the sources standing, and each attempts own skill carries forward what it received, the blueprint in one direction and the framing in the other. Neither source in Figure 12 stands above the targets solo attempt, yet one transfer helps and the other does harm. The p65 TIRx source of DeepSeek-V4-Pro, which passed at 0.997, records 17 Preprint. batched-matmul rewrite tested only on CPU as an open hypothesis with precision caveat. The CuTe DSL skill-conditioned attempt validates float32-promoted variant on CPU and then through GPU grading, runs faster than solo, and records the proposal as validated in its own skill. The p09 CuTe DSL source of GLM-5.3, which failed correctness, records tested scaled dot-product attention (SDPA) interface, mask, and layout rules as route its own attempt had not validated. The TIRx skill-conditioned attempt adopts the route within its first minute, treats its rules as settled, never tries the variable-length flash attention that the solo attempt finds, runs slower than solo, and carries the rules into its own skill. In both cases the target treats the guidance as the source framed it, verifying the hypothesis before use and following the recipe without re-deriving it.

sections.title: E DISCUSSION
sections.content: E.1 LIMITATIONS The findings concern six models transferring skills between CuTe DSL and TIRx on B200 under one agent scaffold, one skill directive, and one per-attempt budget. Source and skill-conditioned attempts come from the same model by design, so the findings do not separate how well model distills its experience from how well it uses it in the other DSL. The content analysis relates transfer outcomes to the presence of content categories, not to individual statements or their wording. The same-problem design holds the relevance of prior experience fixed, so the findings do not cover generalization to new problems or workloads, nor the accumulation of skills over rounds. E.2 FUTURE WORK Comparing source implementations, trajectories, and skills could test how the choice of transferred material affects reuse, while comparing free-form and structured skills with matched content could test how organization affects uptake. Transferring skills between models could separate models ability to distill experience from its ability to use it and could test whether the sources relative standing also predicts transfer from larger models to Flash-tier models. Removing or revising individual guidance statements could test their effects on the target attempts search, verification, and outcome. Transferring skill to related problems in the same family could test which findings still apply when the problem changes and the agent must judge their relevance itself. Chaining transfer across rounds and DSLs could track whether useful knowledge is retained and refined, whether unverified claims are verified, corrected, or propagated, and how these changes affect subsequent attempts.
